title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
raw_text: For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it. That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence. Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud: Workspace MCP servers : Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service. Workspace CLI : Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services. Google Cloud Agent Gateway : A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor. Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs. Consistent controls across every agent workflow Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today: Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum , AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs , paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console , and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately. Getting started Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide , implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum . Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console . Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits. With Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.

title: Enabling zero trust: ALLEN’s move to Chrome Enterprise Premium
raw_text: Editor’s note: Founded in 1988 in Kota, Rajasthan, ALLEN is one of India’s leading coaching institutions, serving over 400,000 students across 350+ classroom campuses in 78 cities. Here, the IT and Cybersecurity Leadership Team shares how they standardized on Chrome Enterprise Premium to secure sensitive data and enable zero trust across over 5,000 users. With a workforce that lives in the browser across a SaaS and multi-cloud estate, securing our digital environment is paramount. Our 5,000+ users include faculty, operations, engineering, contractors, and a large Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) population. Operating at this scale, our top priority is protecting student personally identifiable information (PII) flowing through web applications. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), protecting this data is critical to regulatory compliance and maintaining brand trust. We needed security within the browser. The challenge of a fragmented browser estate We previously operated a mixed-browser environment, but managing multiple browsers made consistent policy enforcement and visibility challenging. We explored several options to standardize; however, our team didn’t want users to have to learn a new tool, and many of the options had high overhead costs. Testing and rolling out Chrome Enterprise Premium We implemented a phased Chrome Enterprise Premium pilot over a few weeks. Our team first validated the management capabilities in the Google Admin console by testing policy, deployment, extension controls, and reporting. Once we felt confident that Chrome Enterprise Premium provided our desired level of visibility, we rolled it out to several hundred users across various environments, including BYOD, Windows, and macOS. We deployed Safe Browsing and URL filtering for immediate threat protection, DLP rules to restrict copy/paste, downloads, and uploads on sensitive SaaS apps, and context-aware access to restrict application entry based on device posture. The proof of concept succeeded across all criteria including consistent policy enforcement, measurable reduction in risky-site and risky-download events, minimal user friction, and a centralized dashboard to give our teams visibility into managed user activity. The real decision moment came when we realized we could achieve a true Zero Trust posture. With Chrome Enterprise Premium as our backbone, access decisions now happen dynamically based on identity, device posture, and context. A teacher on a school-managed laptop enjoys seamless, full access. On a personal phone, that same educator can review materials without compromising security—downloads and clipboard sharing remain locked down. It delivers airtight data protection without disrupting daily instruction. A simpler, stronger foundation With Chrome Enterprise Premium, we replaced virtual desktops (VDIs) and fragmented security tools with built-in browser protection. Securing the browser itself means we no longer need to install heavy security software on every computer. This makes it easy to apply security policies to personal devices used by contractors and employees. Whether our team uses Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, iOS, or Android, we manage updates, policies, and audit reports from a single Google Admin console. Smart access controls Chrome Enterprise Premium ensures we only grant access when it is safe. Every time someone tries to log in, we verify three things: Identity: Is the user signed into their corporate account? Device: Is the laptop or phone managed and secure? Context: Where are they logging in from, and on what network? Stronger data protection We use Chrome Enterprise’s built-in features, such as Safe Browsing sandboxing and site isolation, and auto-updates to keep end users secure while they work on the web. These benefits plus Chrome Enterprise Premium prove that security does not have to slow down business. Employees work without security interruptions, and our IT team gets a single, clear audit trail across all devices. This helps us maintain high efficiency and supports our regulatory compliance efforts. Read more customer stories including how Mercari drove a 50% plus cost reduction with Chrome Enterprise Premium.

title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
raw_text:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data? AlloyDB Omni , Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere. Built-in AI for your local environment AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment. Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8 . No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same. AlloyDB Omni calls a local model server directly from SQL — keeping prompts, data, and responses inside your environment. This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance. Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet. Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time. Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name,

title: Google is named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for SIEM
raw_text: Today, we are proud to announce that Gartner has recognized Google as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM). Among the 15 vendors evaluated this year, Google was positioned furthest on “Completeness of Vision.” Today's threat landscape requires a new approach to security operations that can keep pace with the speed, scale, and sophistication of autonomous attacks. Traditional SIEM architectures centralized logs and alerts, but left analysts to manually stitch together context, write and maintain detections, and craft response playbooks. Now, working alongside analysts, autonomous agents can reason over enterprise context and use frontline threat intelligence to compress detection and response cycles from days to seconds. Advancing the agentic SOC across threat investigation, detection, and response We feel our placement in the 2026 Leaders Quadrant reflects our rapid pace of engineering innovation in Google Security Operations. Since last year’s Magic Quadrant report , we’ve focused on turning the agentic SOC from vision into daily reality for our customers, helping security teams scale their expertise and outpace attackers. Instead, they’re focused on solving complex problems and building proactive protections across our 100-year-old enterprise,” said David Nagel, global CISO, Genuine Parts Company. This can enable organizations to compress the entire end-to-end testing and deployment lifecycle down to under 30 minutes . In addition to streamlining detection engineering, Google Security Operations brings agentic capabilities to threat hunting. Deep threat hunting across months of historical telemetry has historically been a manual, labor-intensive process restricted to specialized hunt teams or senior analysts, often demanding up to a full day of dedicated effort per hunt. title: How Sinch modernized its enterprise data warehouse from Snowflake to BigQuery to power AI
raw_text: As the scale of global communications grows larger and larger, enterprise platforms must process billions of interactions with customers across a complex network of touchpoints without breaking them. A prime example is Sinch , one of the world’s leading cloud communications and customer engagement (CPaaS) companies, which processes billions of customer interactions, SMS routing events, voice calls, and transactional messages. Managing massive international messaging traffic brings significant architectural challenges, so Sinch built a distributed, multi-cloud data footprint across AWS and GCP, with separate Snowflake instances running in the EU, US, and Australia. To eliminate data silos, curb monthly billing spikes, establish a single governed source of truth, and unlock the next generation of predictive AI capabilities, Sinch partnered with Google Cloud Professional Services to migrate its enterprise data warehouse to Google BigQuery . Here’s how we engineered Sinch’s new, modern, cost-efficient, and AI-ready platform architecture The challenge: untangling distributed warehouses and escalating spikes Before it embarked on this modernization journey, Sinch faced several architectural and operational friction points: Cross-regional data sprawl: The company’s separate Snowflake instances in the EU, US, and Australia required intricate inter-region replication, which caused multi-directional dependencies and complex cross-warehouse data management. Resource spikes and commercial inefficiencies: Heavy monthly billing runs drove severe compute spikes in the US, even as other regions had underutilized capacity. High-volume scanning vs. dialect disparities: A single US email event table could generate up to 100 TB of daily scans. Meanwhile, mission-critical SQL relied on Snowflake-specific concurrency and table-swapping paradigms for concurrency validation, which lacked 1:1 equivalents in cloud-native SQL. “Google Cloud's engineering expertise helped us overcome several technical challenges during our migration, particularly around optimising Spark partitioning and restructuring incremental data loads. This allowed us to identify more efficient approaches, improve performance and ensure we built a scalable, reliable solution for the future.” Dan Peters, senior manager, Data Delivery, Sinch Phase 1: validating architecture with a target MVP To mitigate operational risk and prevent downtime for Sinch’s critical enterprise workloads (including ERP and NetSuite integrations), we initiated a phased migration framework: A use case pilot validation: The migration kicked off with a dedicated use case MVP that spanned 20 tables and 125 GB of refined data and automatically validated end-to-end data fidelity. Layered strategy for coupled pipelines: Rather than attempting to cleanly slice interconnected business domains in the EU, the team adopted a layered approach — migrating raw and base (bronze and silver) layers, establishing automated data ingestion, and stabilizing core entities before repointing consumption marts. Orchestration consolidation: Sinch consolidated 36 independent ETL workflows into a single parameterized orchestrator by using Google Cloud Workflows , which streamlined CI/CD deployment logic, and reduced operational overhead. Re-engineering for scale: key architectural pillars 1. Decoupled storage and optimized ingestion Sinch transitioned its data ingestion pipelines to Dataproc Serverless (running Apache Spark 3.5), which directly pulled refined data into native BigQuery tables from S3 and Databricks Unity Catalog. And to overcome batch quota limits and resource exhaustion on billion-row datasets, Sinch optimized jobs by increasing Spark repartitioning factors to 50. For its incremental pipelines, the team eliminated data duplication while minimizing query read costs by replacing slow, keyless merge statements with an optimized insert-and-overwrite windowing strategy. 2. AI-assisted SQL and macro translation In order to accelerate the translation of more than 1,200 dbt models across global projects, Sinch utilized Google Cloud BigQuery Migration Service alongside a set of custom AI translation skills. Here’s how: The team refactored Snowflake-specific table versioning and concurrency management paradigms into deterministic transaction blocks and view abstraction pointers. This ensured atomic updates and consistent data access. Sinch leveraged specialized Google skills for other regional migration — specifically the dbt-sf-to-bq-translator skill powered by the underlying BigQuery Translation API — to automate the conversion of dbt models from Snowflake to BigQuery SQL syntax. This significantly reduced manual refactoring effort and error rates. Concurrency checks that relied on row-level locking were redesigned into serialized batch validations. Integer overflow risks in massive calculation tables were solved by adopting a tiered precision strategy (favoring NUMERIC over BIGNUMERIC ), which cut storage costs and preserved absolute precision. “Migrating over a thousand complex dbt models and translating legacy SQL required a robust, automated approach. Google Cloud's guidance on query restructuring helped us streamline pipeline development and remove compilation blockers. The team shared best practices for migrating code from Snowflake to BigQuery, such as replacing Snowflake SWAP WITH and hybrid-table patterns with BigQuery time travel. They also helped us build workflows that copy data from Snowflake to BigQuery and run our dbt jobs along the way, which sped up our move to BigQuery.” Varun Gupta, Senior Data Engineer, Sinch Real-world business impact By completing the migration, Sinch successfully transformed the operational bottleneck of its global data footprint into a driver of enterprise growth: Metric / capability Before (Snowflake) After (BigQuery) Pipeline performance High data churn; lengthy multi-hour batch runs Significantly faster query and pipeline processing speeds across billions of records Compute and billing efficiency Unpredictable month-end billing spikes Predictable capacity management with BigQuery reservations and slot autoscaling AI readiness Segmented data warehouses requiring external pipelines Native BQML and Vertex AI decision intelligence platform Looking ahead With its core European warehouse workloads stabilized on BigQuery and data validation consistently outperforming legacy benchmarks, Sinch is now expanding this modern blueprint across its Australian (SMB) and US analytics. The SMB instance migration is already in progress and is utilizing Antigravity skills for the Snowflake to BigQuery translation. By unifying data storage, operational governance, and serverless compute, Sinch has built a resilient platform that delivers real-time messaging reliability today while positioning the company to capture the full potential of enterprise AI tomorrow.

title: Check Point security management servers hit in global cyberattack campaign
raw_text: An active intrusion campaign targeting Check Point security management servers has been uncovered, with confirmed attack activity observed between October 17 and November 2, 2026, impacting 22 organizations globally. Tracked by cybersecurity firm GreyNoise as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), the campaign does not appear to be focused on a single region or industry. Impacted organizations span assets across the US, the UK, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, and Australia, across sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. “The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique,” a Check Point spokesperson said. “Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity. The most important action is to install the available updates for CVE-2026-16232. Check Point has already released fixes and detailed mitigation and investigation guidance in its SecureKnowledge advisory.” GreyNoise has not attributed GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group. “An intrusion into a Check Point security management server is particularly serious because it is not just another server in the enterprise network. It effectively acts as the central control point for managing an organisation’s firewall infrastructure and security policies, with highly privileged access,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. He said that depending on the deployment and the level of access obtained, the consequences could extend well beyond the security infrastructure itself, potentially exposing sensitive data and critical business applications and disrupting enterprise operations. Building the relay infrastructure The threat actor operated across 99 IP addresses, primarily routed outbound through ExpressVPN or compromised Check Point devices, generating more than 1,400 network sessions, over 800 command-line artifacts, and over 1,200 created, uploaded, or downloaded files. GreyNoise first observed the actor scanning and exploiting a Rejetto HFS server on October 2, 2026. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returned a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm and thus recover an HFS session cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allowed the attacker to log in as admin without a password. A few minutes later, GreyNoise observed that admin requests with forged session cookies were used to gain control of the server. This led GreyNoise to believe that exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The forged cookie contained “allow_session_ip_change:true”, allowing forged cookies to work from any IP address. On October 5, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server, the research said. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Three days later, on October 8, the threat actor automation check in to the compromised server using the HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Instead of using SSH access right away, on October 19, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. GreyNoise noted that it believes the idea was to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations. As the malware download failed, the threat actor returned with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay the next day. On October 20, the threat actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_.py) for setting up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, which they used to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from a scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point security management server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets. The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy. Targeted intrusion Once the compromised server was established as a relay, the actor used it to manage interactions with previously compromised Check Point devices, actively deepening their intrusion against Victim A while conducting bulk actions across 21 other victim organizations. Across the campaign, the operator relied on at least 30 Python scripts, including helpers, launchers, vulnerability probes, and exploit runners. Between October 20 and 26, the attacker had a compromised Victim A asset download and run Chisel in client mode, allowing them to further scan and interact with Victim A’s environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232, the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point management servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix NetScaler , Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter , Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers. Between October 20 and 21, the attacker focused on Victim A, first using exploit.py (CVE-2026-16232) against one Check Point server before scanning a second with spray_portal.py. When that second device failed to report back to the relay box, the actor created pull_.py to steal credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configurations through the first compromised server. The attacker then expanded inside Victim A’s network, running broad port scans with curl, telnet, nmap, and a domain controller probe, followed by targeted exploits against internal Microsoft Netlogon, Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, Microsoft Exchange, and VMware vCenter servers. They wrapped up this phase by running comb.py,ssh_comb.py, and ssh_spray.py populated with victim-themed usernames and passwords. On October 26, the operation shifted to bulk targeting. The actor issued a bulk certificate management task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers, including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. Results were shipped in a text file to the hop server that contained an incrementing IP order to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers and deliver them via SCP to this exfil folder. Although the task failed on every device, the error logs sent back to the hop server exposed victim IP addresses and revealed an /etc/ld.so.preload reference to /usr/lib/.libproc.so, pointing to a likely implant before activity paused until November 2. GreyNoise suspects the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus including separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting. Securing the management plane Although GreyNoise’s direct visibility into the campaign paused around November 2, 2026, security leaders must still verify whether their environments have been quietly infiltrated. With attackers planting backdoors on breached Check Point servers, CISOs must audit their environments for signs of quiet compromise. To establish whether Check Point infrastructure has been compromised, CISOs and security teams should examine administrative login records for unusual access patterns, including unfamiliar IP addresses, unexpected login times, and unauthorised access added Dhar. They should also look for changes to firewall policies, access-control rules, and configuration files, and thoroughly review system logs, audit trails, and command execution history for suspicious activity. Dhar noted that once there are indications of a compromise, the immediate priority should be to prevent further access and contain the damage. Security teams should restrict access to the management server to authorised administrative systems and isolate confirmed compromised systems while preserving forensic evidence. Unauthorised accounts should be disabled, suspicious SSH keys and access tokens revoked, and identified malicious IP addresses and domains blocked.

title: Prompting AI to be ‘thorough’ can drive sandbox escapes, Anthropic says
raw_text: Prompt wording meant to make AI agents more resourceful, such as telling them to search thoroughly or invoking authority, sharply raises the odds they will reach outside a poorly secured sandbox, Anthropic has found in its latest evaluation. The evaluation, called Siren, gives Claude models routine dev-ops tasks inside deliberately weakened sandboxes and places a “honeypot,” such as a credential, file, or emulated internet service, outside the boundary, Anthropic researchers Oscar O’Rahilly and Darya Kaviani wrote in a blog post . Anthropic tested six Claude models, from Mythos 5 to the 5.5 series, without the safeguards that ship in its products. The tests covered more than 1,700 scenarios in 26 sandboxes built on tools including Docker, gVisor, and QEMU. Most of the weaknesses are misconfigurations modeled on public reports, the company said. Wording mattered more than deadlines Anthropic’s researchers tested different types of instructions, which they called “tempters”. Some increased urgency by introducing deadlines or the consequences of failure. Others encouraged agents to search extensively or gave them broad authority over their machines. “Some tempters give the model broad authority over its own machine. Others tell it to search thoroughly, on that machine or more widely, and list what it checked,” the researchers wrote. Removing deadlines and stated costs of failure changed the rate of reaching outside by no more than about six percentage points, the post said. Removing the wording that asked for thoroughness and asserted authority had a far larger effect, cutting reach rates by 23 to 26 points in five of the six models, the researchers wrote. Claude Mythos 5 was the exception, reaching outside about 90% of the time in every version of the scenarios, the post added. Across the Claude 5.5 models and Claude Mythos 5.2, agents reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios, but misaligned use occurred in only 0.6% to 1.6%. The corresponding misaligned-use rates for the older Claude Mythos 5 and 5.1 models were 25.8% and 12.7%, respectively, according to the post. “Siren is designed to make this behavior easy to measure; its rates are not an estimate of how often this behavior happens in real use,” the company wrote. Six rules in the system prompt The first mitigation Anthropic tested was spelling out six sandbox rules in the system prompt. They cover host files, host services, container engine sockets, credentials, network destinations, and anything left running on the host after a task ends. The rules made the models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside, cutting the rate for the newest models to about 2% or less, the researchers wrote. Mythos 5 still reached outside in nearly a quarter of scenarios. Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said no CISO should rely solely on system prompt rules as a control for agents. “It’s like marking your own homework: asking a model to moderate itself is a high-risk approach,” Brown said. Mitigations reduce boundary crossing Anthropic tested three measures to reduce the likelihood of agents reaching outside their sandboxes. The first involved explicitly describing the sandbox, specifying which resources were off-limits, and instructing the model to stop and report if a task required resources it had not been given. This reduced reaching-out rates by 68% to 96%, depending on the model. A tool allowing agents to report sandbox weaknesses rather than exploit them reduced the rate by seven to 33 percentage points. The third measure, auto mode, uses a classifier to check tool calls before execution. In an offline replay of the test episodes, it blocked the first command accessing external material in 96% to 100% of misaligned use cases. It blocked the first command attempting to reach outside in 53% to 84% of boundary-crossing episodes. The mitigations make escape less likely but “don’t fix the sandbox itself,” Anthropic wrote. Brown said enterprises should not rely on AI vendors to secure their own models. Instead, they should encase agents in a governance structure that limits scope and access to what is required and no more, he said. “CISOs may use AI to govern AI, but they must ensure that the governance AI is from a different vendor and has a different model provenance than the one they are governing,” Brown said. Models suspect they are being tested Anthropic also found that models frequently suspected they were being tested. Claude Sonnet 5.5 showed signs of evaluation awareness in 67% of scenarios. Across the four newer models, the rate ranged from 43% to 67%. “With only six models, we can’t tell whether models are more cautious about reaching outside because they suspect they are in a test, or whether the increased eval awareness and the reduced tendency to leave the sandbox are both products of how newer models were trained,” the researchers wrote. Brown said enterprises should not rely on vendor-produced evaluations alone when deciding whether to deploy agents. “Agents are goal-focused and will stop at nothing to achieve their mission,” he said. Organisations should instead deploy agents with “an identified sponsor, a clear scope, an expiry date and an evidential record of what the agent actually did.”

title: Despite doom and gloom headlines, AI attacks are thin on the ground
raw_text: When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses before the public — and attackers — got their hands on the technology. Soon after, AI companies, one after the other, warned that their AI models were smart enough to discover previously unknown exploits and escape containment. And a new worldview took hold, that security organizations were soon to see a wave of new kinds of attacks, never seen before, and every company was at risk — unless it immediately started using the latest and greatest AI to defend against all these new threats. Has that happened? Well, kind of. What CISOs are seeing In the first quarter of 2026, RSAC asked Fortune 1000 CISOs whether they’d seen definitive evidence of AI-powered attack techniques being used against their companies, beyond social engineering, and 44% said yes. “We asked the same question in Q4 of a similar cohort,” says Laura Koetzle, RSAC’s head of community research. According to preliminary results — the survey isn’t complete yet — nearly 58% now say they’ve seen evidence of AI-powered attack techniques. As a result, the majority of CISOs are revamping their vulnerability management programs, according to the forthcoming survey. But they’re not upending how they approach cybersecurity, Koetzle adds. “The same foundational principles still apply.” The main difference today is in speed and quantity, she says. Lincoln Wallen, CTO at Framestore, an Academy Award–winning visual effects company, isn’t turning a blind eye to what AI could be used for by attackers. “We take the potential very seriously,” he says. But he’s taking an old-school approach to dealing with this new threat. “We’re putting a lot of emphasis on cleanliness, hygiene, and patching.” So far, the signs of AI use have been limited to more sophisticated phishing attacks, he says. “They feel anecdotally more well put-together, more convincing, involving many more disparate elements of data,” he says. “That’s the most concrete thing that we’ve seen.” To deal with that, the company has updated its anti-phishing training. Another area that Framestore is investing in is more efficient and prioritized patching and more frequent penetration testing. Enhanced productivity but familiar threats The data seems to support Framestore’s approach, even if the headlines don’t. Last week, headlines quoted Google’s announcement that “ the era of autonomous attacks had arrived ” — a reference to Google’s original blog post teaser to its latest AI Threat Tracker report. But in the actual report , John Hultquist, chief analyst at the Google Threat Intelligence Group, seemed to undercut this top line teaser, saying: “For the most part, attackers aren’t using new groundbreaking methods to break into systems — they are still going after known, unfixed issues, just with much greater speed and scale.” (Google later changed its headline to “ Outpace automated cyber threats with security built for nonstop defense .”) According to Google’s report, the mechanics of intrusion remain the same. Even attackers using new AI-powered attack frameworks are using them to leverage compromised credentials and unpatched systems. It’s the speed and scale at which these frameworks can be used that’s the challenge. In fact, using LLMs can even hurt the attackers, as the frameworks “trade stealth for velocity,” researchers say. The attacks can be “forensically noisy” and can hallucinate non-existent details or targets. “Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don’t.” Or, as Sergej Epp summed up as a takeaway from a recent Cloud Security Alliance CISO huddle call on autonomous attacks, “detecting these attacks is — at least for now — not the hard part. They make a lot of noise, like 1000 interns.” Austin Berglas, managing director and head of cyber operations at Nardello & Co., a global investigations firm, says he’s not seeing AI-discovered zero days or self-replicating AI agents out in the wild. “This is one of those examples that is still in the lab environment,” he says. Most attackers are using AI the way everyone does, he says. “Just like individuals use it for their daily productivity and efficiency, same with the bad actors. They’re able to scale, do it cheaper, do it quicker. And you’re seeing people who typically wouldn’t have the technical chops to do something, who are now able to do it because AI can do the technical side.” The industry is seeing evidence of faster weaponization of vulnerabilities, confirms Gartner analyst John Watts. “Where it starts to have less evidence is for fully autonomous attacks. What happened with Hugging Face is a fully autonomous attack, and that isn’t that common.” How CISOs should respond But if the wave of autonomous attacks and AI-powered malware hasn’t yet fully arrived, what should CISOs do given the reality on the ground? “The feedback that we get from our client base is that they believe there’s a lot of value in using the controls they already have,” Gartner’s Watts says. “The wake-up call for the practitioners is to get busy with the patching,” confirms Paul Webber, an analyst at Software Analyst Cyber Research, adding that security by obscurity is no longer an option. The biggest problem enterprises are facing, he notes, is that they need better automation to handle the increased workload, and the tools aren’t yet where they need to be. “People need more trust in the security tools so they can move from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop towards fully autonomous response,” Webber says. “And that’s going to take some discipline, some standardization, and some proof in the efficacy of the security tools themselves. At the moment, they’re neither built to a specific standard or definition and people are being asked to make purchasing decisions without physical proof that the tools can do what they purport to do.” And, in some ways, the much-lauded defensive AI capabilities can make things worse — such as by exposing legacy vulnerabilities that companies now have to hurry up and patch, on top of their already large backlog. “This is a conversation that we’re actively having right now,” says Christina Powers, partner and cybersecurity consulting leader at West Monroe, a management consulting firm. “We’re working with a mid-sized bank, and they are just completely lost on how to keep up with the number of vulnerabilities that they got,” she says. “They’re sitting on millions of vulnerabilities. They don’t even know where to start. There’s a bit of analysis paralysis that’s happening because there’s so much information coming in.” The tools are improving all the time, Powers says, but she recommends security leaders not to wait for better technology to come along. “If you’re sitting and waiting, you become more of a target because you’re falling behind,” she says.

Soon after, AI companies, one after the other, warned that their AI models were smart enough to discover previously unknown exploits and escape containment. And a new worldview took hold, that security organizations were soon to see a wave of new kinds of attacks, never seen before, and every company was at risk — unless it immediately started using the latest and greatest AI to defend against all these new threats. Has that happened?

title: Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
raw_text: Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries. In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset. The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual. Need to buy time “For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint,” Cisco president and CPO Jeetu Patel wrote in a blog post . “You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it.” But, he asserted, this approach is “fundamentally mismatched” to AI. Security should live inside the infrastructure itself. “If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind,” he said. He noted that AI agents are getting better at discovering security vulnerabilities; for instance, startup Calif used AI to help discover the PHP2Shell flaw and a major Java bug . Dovetailing with this, the agents themselves are both a risk vector and an adversarial actor. Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he pointed out. Flaws unfold over minutes and hours, as opposed to the days and weeks of the past, but permanent fixes take time to build, test, and roll out. “We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place,” Patel said. Making the infrastructure secure from the start Shirudo combines Cisco’s infrastructure with OpenAI’s frontier models and AI research. It is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which supports the running of small, sandboxed programs inside a Linux kernel without changing source code or loading additional modules. “This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems,” OpenAI explained in its blog post announcing the project . Speaking in their own language, guardian agents investigate and detect flaws and build shields, then test whether they stop the attack, all without disrupting the targeted service. The shields are cryptographically signed and only loaded when verified and deemed safe. Linux’s eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against safety rules, and kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Shirudo also uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being added or removed. All this takes place even if attackers have already gained access to a system. Further, self-defending agents can monitor for false positives, performance, and overall system health, and incorporate red-team findings and other feedback as well as signals for continuous improvement. Evidence backing every control travels across the system. The idea, according to Cisco and OpenAI, is to make the infrastructure itself secure by default. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer,” OpenAI wrote in its post. Shirudo in the wild Shirudo has its roots in Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform developed and open-sourced by Isovalent, which was acquired by Cisco in 2024 . It is already incorporated into Cisco’s Live Protect capability. But Tetragon has been rewritten for the agentic era; its previous iteration pointed AI to human-oriented consoles, configuration files, and policy languages. In that workflow, the agent thought in machine code, which was then decoded for humans and processed, then translated back again into machine code. With Shirudo, agents interact in their natural language, which is code. “Agents are different,” Isovalent co-founder Thomas Graf and its chief open source officer Liz Rice noted in a blog post : They are very good at generating code, can absorb huge amounts of context quickly, and “[don’t] mind reverse engineering several million lines of assembly code.” In one controlled testing environment, researchers fed information about the Java4Shell vulnerability into Shirudo, which automatically created a shield against exploitation, generating a mitigation in Java bytecode which was injected into any Java app and added validation on the base64 input to guard against exploit attempts by threat actors. Graf and Rice explained that agent loops can either be tasked to actively search for new vulnerabilities on their own, or work off external sources like newly-available security disclosures. Agents can generate mitigation code, reproduce and validate exploits, and determine the most effective patching measures. This step is repeated until the agent identifies a successful path. The shield is then signed and securely rolled out to vulnerable nodes; it retires when a patch is installed. “This step is continuously monitored and repeated to achieve the highest possible security score while closely monitoring the health of applications,” Graf and Rice explained. It can be designed to be “more or less autonomous.” Once mitigation shields are deployed, the system employs a “hit” count of active exploitation attempts, so that exploits can be investigated on demand. Ultimately, the Shirudo project is only the beginning, Graf and Rice noted, but it already shows “true potential” and the hope is it will continue to evolve in the open source ecosystem. “We believe that building secure infrastructure for the AI era is an industry-scale problem,” they said. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, a permissive open-source software license approved by the Open Source Initiative. This allows anyone to use, modify, and redistribute software, including in proprietary or commercial products, with minimal restrictions. Its BPF programs are dual licensed under GPL and BSD. Developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators are encouraged to inspect the code, test outcomes, and contribute to the project’s development. title: Attackers exploited an Azure API Management flaw to steal secrets, Microsoft warns
raw_text: Microsoft is warning customers that attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to steal stored secrets, an intrusion that Norway’s National Security Authority has linked to breaches at two energy companies and says organizations should assume exposed credentials were compromised. Microsoft said in an Azure Service Health security advisory sent to customers that it identified the vulnerability on Nov. 18 and deployed a mitigation the following day. The advisory, tracking ID MZK9-GH0, said the exposure began before Microsoft found the flaw, reported Bleeping Computer. The company said in the advisory that “an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances.” The potentially exposed information includes secrets stored in Named Values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs, the report added. Microsoft warned that its mitigation does not invalidate previously compromised credentials and that affected customers must rotate potentially exposed secrets and investigate suspicious activity. “We identified and fixed a security issue affecting the Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium tiers of Azure API Management (APIM) Classic. Azure API Management v2 tiers are not affected,” a Microsoft spokesperson said. The potential exposure was not limited to a theoretical security risk. Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an operational environment. Norway tells customers to assume exposure In a security advisory published November 20 and updated November 23, NSM said an unidentified actor had actively targeted access tokens, secrets, and Named Values stored in Azure API Management. “Earlier this week, NSM became aware of a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) that affects several Norwegian businesses,” NSM said in the advisory, translated from Norwegian. It said the vulnerability should now be closed, but asked organizations to take measures anyway. “Anyone with Azure API Manager must assume that their secrets and named values ​​are out of whack,” the advisory added. “This means that the business must roll back all tokens and secrets.” In the advisory, NSM’s director of operational cybersecurity, Martin Albert-Hoff, said the vulnerability was first discovered by Norway’s energy sector. The agency identified Equinor and Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations and said the vulnerability had also affected organizations in other countries and sectors. Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems on November 17. In an update published November 20 , the company said the attack had been stopped, production was running normally, and there was no indication that data had been stolen or altered. A day later, Skagerak Energi reported an attempted cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the incident had not affected its operations or production and that there was no indication that information had been compromised. NSM warned that public disclosure of the vulnerability could encourage additional threat actors to attempt exploitation. “When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors may attempt to exploit it,” the agency said in its advisory (translated from Norwegian), adding that the rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence was affecting the threat environment. Neither Microsoft’s advisory nor NSM’s notice includes a CVE identifier for the flaw. Urgent need to rotate credentials Microsoft’s mitigation closed the unauthorized management-plane access path, but it advised customers to investigate whether their APIM instances were accessed before the fix and whether stored credentials could have been exposed, the report added. In a November 21 post on its Azure Integration Services blog , Microsoft published guidance on identifying and rotating credentials configured in Azure API Management. The guidance covers subscription keys, Named Values containing secrets, backend credentials, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect client secrets, connection strings, and credentials written directly into API policies. Microsoft recommended that organizations rotate credentials at the systems where they were originally issued, rather than simply updating their values in APIM. “Updating the value in API Management alone does not invalidate the old credential,” the company said in the blog post, as per the report. NSM has issued more extensive recommendations, advising organizations using Azure API Management to assume that their secrets and Named Values may have been exposed and to rotate all associated tokens and secrets. The agency also published a patch check. According to NSM, instances on the 0.52.x branch are patched from build 31936, and those on 0.53.x are from build 31938. V2 and Consumption tier instances are not vulnerable, the agency said. Organizations with unpatched instances should contact Microsoft directly, and those that see signs of compromise should contact NSM, the advisory said. Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen, who published detection and hunting guidance after the advisories, said patching alone is not enough. “If you run APIM, patching isn’t the end of it,” Kristiansen wrote in a blog post. His rotation list includes backend credentials, app registration secrets, subscription keys, the Key Vault secrets the service references, and tenant access keys. Microsoft did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

title: The right people in the room: Getting leaders on board with DEI
raw_text:
Over the past five years, there has been a clear disparity in which organisations have claimed to be on top of improving diversity in tech, yet the reality of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) across the tech industry as a whole has remained very different.

Research has previously suggested a large number of people across Europe believe women are well represented in tech leadership positions, and tech workers have claimed in the past that they believe DEI initiatives are working.

You don’t have to dig very deep, however, to find figures in direct contrast to this. In 2024, the now-defunct Tech Talent Charter found women made up only 21% of senior tech leaders in the UK within its signatories, representing firms already on board with DEI. Frank Recruitment Group found women only made up a quarter of CIO positions in FTSE 100 companies in 2023.

The percentage of women working in tech roles currently stands at around 22%, according to research from BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT, but progress is so slow that this number only increased by three percentage points between 2020 and 2025.

Currently, the overwhelming majority of those in leadership positions in the technology sector are white, middle-aged men.

Some men at Computer Weekly’s diversity event even admitted to “getting bored of the same kind of conversations and perspectives that we’re surrounded by” – so there’s an appetite for change.

There was also the suggestion that more women seek to take on non-executive directorships and chair positions, like many of the women who are on Computer Weekly’s list of the most influential women in UK tech, so they can begin to have a say as part of business leadership.

But one expert pointed out that we can’t always “trust or rely” on those at the top, male or female, to “have our best interests at heart in terms of supporting diversity”, so we need to try other ways to get those in leadership positions on side.

“It’s really just about trying different approaches and different ways,” they said. “Different people respond to different information.”

Speak their language

“We’ve talked about how it’s ethical to prioritise diversity, but that doesn’t always land as a reason for actually turning that into actions at leadership level. Think about how you connect it to a commercial reason.”

Regardless of what is right, most organisations are driven by profit, so highlighting how a diverse tech workforce will make or save a business money is the easiest way to get leaders on side.

One expert attending the event pointed out that this could be achieved by asking leaders to consider whether their customers are asking questions about the make-up of its teams, and how this may affect winning contracts.

If having diverse teams could increase the customer base of a business, it’s worth investing in – and research has found ethical practices such as ensuring diversity in an organisation is becoming increasingly important for younger people as they enter employment and make their way up the ranks.

This also means firms have more to lose if their culture doesn’t meet the needs of new hires – recruiting, training and onboarding is expensive, especially if a firm subsequently loses people as a result of poor culture.

Cost savings could also be an incentive to hire internally, potentially tackling the issue found in the recent Lovelace report, whereby women are leaving their technology roles every year due to a lack of opportunities to advance their careers.

Another expert at Computer Weekly’s event explained there may be scope to look at people who have been in the organisation for a certain amount of time without moving role, and have potential to step up or sideways, but who may otherwise leave the business and then have to be replaced. Hiring internally for experienced roles and filling gaps with entry-level hires is cheaper than bringing in someone externally with many years of experience who may hit the ground running, but who may not be able to innovate or bring different ideas to the business.

Experts mentioned several types of datasets that could be helpful for getting leadership on board with DEI.

Keeping track of talent pipelines was one area where data could be useful – who has been in their role for a certain amount of time and may leave without advancement; what does the diversity of your talent look like; where are you losing talent? One delegate said visualisation of such data can help leadership look beyond solely the ethical side of DEI and into the business benefits.

Finally, experts pointed out that targets are a language that management understand, and making representation a target for hiring managers alongside financial targets has been a strategy suggested many times over the years. If it can be measured and held accountable, it gets done.

“We talked about the importance of persistence. If you’re telling the story of diversity and inclusion, you have to keep going back.”

Getting the right people in the room to advance diversity in the tech space can present as a catch-22. You need diverse minds at the top to push for equality and make a difference, but those people aren’t currently represented, so how can we get them in the right roles?  

Nothing changes overnight, and experts at this year’s DEI event emphasised the need for persistence, to “keep telling that story”, whether from the perspective of recruitment practices, reward systems, data or financial incentives.

“Different areas within the business have different mindsets; different perspectives,” one delegate said, so the above recommendations may carry more or less weight depending who you approach.

Ultimately, how these recommendations are received and acted upon depends on the culture of an organisation.

Audience members pointed out that it can be difficult pushing for diversity – especially as an individual. This is even more true if the culture of an organisation means such warnings and requests fall on deaf ears.

People are fatigued by the slow rate of change, but managers, teams, companies and individuals all need to keep pushing for DEI, finding the right language to speak to leaders to shift their thinking in the right direction, and begin to get the right people into the right rooms.

Glick urged: “This is a relentless thing. We just have to keep going. We have to keep knocking on doors and opening doors, and getting through those doors. The more and more that happens, the more progress we’ll make.”

title: The five things private equity wants from software companies in the age of AI
raw_text:
Software leaders preparing for a sale or investment face a tougher set of questions than they did two years ago. Worried that AI might make some software products redundant, what investors want from software companies is evidence. Evidence that customers depend on the product, evidence that AI features pay for themselves, and evidence that the leadership team can turn technology into results.

 So, what do software businesses need to focus on in order to maximise the chances of securing private equity (PE) investment? From our conversations and diligence work with PE investors, I see five points as key:

1. Investors need assurance and want to talk to your customers

AI is steadily cutting the cost of writing software. As code gets cheaper to produce, it therefore becomes a weaker source of advantage. As a result, value shifts to being indispensable to the customer's workflow, being embedded in daily processes, and controlling the data, relationships and trust needed to get work done.

Investors won’t just take a software company’s word for it that their product won’t be superseded by AI. Potential buyers and investors now increasingly check that by talking to customers. Be prepared for this and anticipate the conversation. 

2. AI features must pay their way

Anecdotal experience suggests that around half of enterprise software companies now offer some form of generative or agentic AI in their products. But maturity varies widely. Many features are search, summaries or chat assistants that support a workflow but are hard to tie to a return. A smaller group uses agents that complete multi-step tasks for users.

 The cost side often gets underestimated, with a danger that companies misjudge how quickly the use of AI and running costs grow, often giving AI features away for free. Three key investor concerns here are:

  • Will customers pay more for AI features?
  • Do they improve retention or productivity?
  • Does the value created exceed the cost of delivering it?

 As AI providers start charging, model costs are likely to move into the cost of sales and put pressure on gross margins. Being able to show that products are still profitable even with AI costs included is another critical factor in the investor conversation.

3. Show AI is making your own business more efficient

Investors will look at how you use AI inside your own business, not just in your product. AI-native entrants are building software with smaller teams and lower cost bases, so much of the competition they bring will be on price. Established software suppliers need to show they can match that efficiency, and investors will want evidence of it, not just plans.

 That means showing where AI is used internally (software development, testing, customer support and back-office functions) and what it has delivered. That could be faster release cycles, more output per developer, a lower cost to serve, or costs that no longer grow in line with revenue. Measurements taken before rollout and tracked since will count for far more than anecdotes or the number of AI licences bought.

 Be realistic about the limits, though. AI largely creates gains in routine coding and testing; it does not solve technical debt in old or legacy systems. In BearingPoint's experience, AI won't remove a technical-debt problem from an investor's assessment. If parts of the platform need modernising, be honest about it, because buyers will still want it measured, costed and given a realistic timeline.

4. Make sure customers can realise the value

 Adding AI features is not enough – you need to make sure your customers can successfully adopt them and translate them into measurable value. That means understanding the customer’s workflows, identifying where the product or AI capability creates a meaningful improvement, and then helping customers embed it into the way they operate (which may include designing software their own agents can use effectively).

 This may require a change in go-to-market models too. Rather than relying primarily on traditional support, vendors may need more customer-success specialists, domain experts or forward-deployed technical teams who can help customers redesign workflows, integrate AI capabilities and track the value being created.

 For investors, the important evidence is not simply that these capabilities exist. Software companies should be able to demonstrate adoption, increased product usage, measurable customer outcomes and ultimately stronger retention or expansion. Those evidence points can show a repeatable model for turning product capability into customer value and help convince investors that there is long-term value for customers buying your product, rather than choosing to build it.

5. Leadership is critical

AI is an organisational challenge even more than it is a technical one. Leadership should take collective responsibility for successfully building AI into the software strategy. It is clear direction from the board, with functional leaders accountable for specific outcomes, that most often makes the difference. Ultimately, the way that AI is led, managed and governed is one of the critical determinants for PE investors – something they look at almost above everything else. Value remains human, you might say, even if it is delivered through technology.

Moving forward

For software leaders, the message is not to slow down on AI – but to tighten up. The businesses investors favour will be those able to show where they are embedded in the customer's workflow, what AI is worth after its costs, how efficiently they run themselves, and how leadership turns it into measurable results.

title: Authorised payment fraud up 22%, but ‘nobody answers’ why police aren’t resourced to fight it
raw_text:
Almost half of the money taken from UK bank accounts through fraud in the first half of this year was authorised by the victims themselves, according to figures from UK Finance.

The finance industry body is calling for tech and telecoms companies to do more to stop fraud, but a financial services veteran with years of experience fighting fraud said people are ignoring the fact that the police lack the resources to catch the fraudsters.

A total of £660m was stolen from UK bank accounts in the first six months of 2026, with £316m of this authorised by tricked customers, according to UK Finance figures. This was 22% higher than the same period last year.

In contrast, unauthorised fraud, where criminals steal money without customers approving transactions, fell by 8%, to £343m.

UK Finance, which represents banks, reported that 58% of what are known as authorised push payment (APP) fraud cases started online, and 16% started through telecommunication networks. APP fraud occurs when criminals use fake websites, emails and phone numbers to trick consumers into authorising payments to them. Because payment is authorised, it bypasses the security systems banks have in place to prevent fraud.

This is further evidence that fraudsters are increasingly using social media to trick customers rather than attempting to get around bank security. In the UK Finance survey, banks reported preventing about £810m of unauthorised fraud, nearly two-and-a-half times the amount criminals stole.

UK Finance is continuing to call for stronger fraud prevention obligations on technology and telecommunications companies.

  • APP fraud reimbursement proposal is ‘fundamentally flawed’, say MPs.
  • Santander calls for cooperation to tackle APP fraud.
  • Banking regulatory body wants a ‘tripwire’ to flag APP fraud.

Ruth Ray, managing director of economic crime at the trade group, said the financial services industry invests heavily in protecting consumers.

“But criminals are increasingly exploiting online platforms and telecommunications networks to target and manipulate victims before a payment is ever made,” she added.

“The financial services sector cannot tackle this threat alone,” said Ray. “We need stronger obligations on technology and telecommunications firms so that every sector exploited by fraudsters is held accountable and plays its part in preventing harm.”

Santander UK’s head of fraud prevention, Chris Ainsley, agreed. “It’s encouraging to see that banks are helping to protect customers by preventing more money being stolen than is being lost to fraud,” he said. “But it’s clear that other sectors must step up to help cut scams off at source.”

To catch a thief

But inadequate policing is a major issue, according to forensic investigator Ron Warmington, a former global head of banking investigations at Citibank. He said part of the problem is that fraudsters rarely get caught, due to a lack of police resources.

Warmington said overall fraud makes up a huge proportion of total crime, but only a relatively small slice of resources are applied to catching fraudsters. “They rarely get caught, so if their frauds fail, they just try again,” he added.

According to a Public Accounts Committee report in 2023, despite making up 41% of all crime in the year to June 2022, only around 1% of police personnel were dedicated to fraud. That same year, a Justice Committee report said fraud accounted for more than 40% of all crime, but only 2% of police resources are allocated to fraud. 

Warmington said: “The question nobody answers is this: If nearly half of reported crime is fraud, what is the percentage of police resources applied to fighting it?”

Banks being forced to reimburse customers that fall prey to APP fraudsters also fails to stop the criminals investing in more innovative ways of conning people.

Jonathan Frost, director of global advisory for security supplier BioCatch, said: “Reimbursement protects victims, but it does not stop criminals getting paid. To reverse the trend, we need to make fraud less profitable in the first place.

“Criminals exploit the gaps between banks, social media platforms and telecoms networks, relying on mule accounts to move stolen funds,” he said. “Banks must detect manipulation earlier, identify suspicious receiving accounts and share risk intelligence across institutions in real time, before the money moves.”
