title: Amazon CTO Werner Vogels: Computing to converge with biology
raw_text:
Technology must decode how biology handles information, because nature handles vast amounts of data with a fraction of the energy used in datacentres.

Meanwhile, security and sovereignty need to be built into systems and software at their inception, and scientists will find new cures for diseases that were unattainable before artificial intelligence (AI).

And to top all of this, new ways for humans to interface with information systems will lead to IT that can read our minds.

Those are the short versions of Amazon chief technology officer Werner Vogels’ predictions for 2027. He unveiled them this week, and started with a word he said now outranks “AI” as the term of the moment. That word is “human”.

“Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year is ‘human’ – it’s not ‘AI’, it’s not ‘artificial’, it’s ‘human’,” said Vogels.

He described himself as “a technology optimist”, but also “a realist”. “I believe we build technology not for technology’s sake, but to support humans, to make our lives better,” he said.

Vogels has spent 22 years as Amazon’s chief technology officer. His 2026 predictions, published this time last year, included the dawn of the renaissance developer – developers who blend creativity and technical expertise, like Leonardo da Vinci.

1. Computing should take its lead from biology

Vogels’ first prediction is that computing will “return to biology” to learn how to use far fewer resources. The trigger, he said, is the enormous resource usage of today’s AI models, which need “millions of central processing units [CPUs] and graphics processing units [GPUs] – massive data storage”. The human brain does the same job far more cheaply. “Our brain, even with the 86 billion neurons in it, only uses 20 watts,” said Vogels.

On a 2023 trip to Melbourne, he visited Cortical Labs, where human neurons grown on silicon learned tasks by trial and error. Its first installations came online this summer, each built on the CL1, “a self-contained computer that keeps living human neurons alive on a silicon chip”. A CL1 holds about 200,000 neurons and runs on 25 to 30 watts.

“A full rack of 30 draws under 1,000 watts, while a rack of high-end GPUs requires more than 600 kilowatts,” said Vogels.

Brain-inspired chips at the University of Texas at Dallas learn by strengthening connections when neurons on either side fire together – “Hebbian learning” – which suits edge computing, where “a little chip that sits in the tyre of your car” keeps learning how you drive.

“The next major breakthrough in computing will come from understanding how biology does more with less,” he said.

Asked how society should weigh AI’s cost, Vogels said resource use matters most. “Even the smallest LLMs [large language models] take enormous amounts of energy to just train, and inference is not free,” he said. “The more we can reduce the resource usage and the cheaper we can make this, the more we have an opportunity to make all of this technology available for everyone, not just for the largest, biggest companies.” That, Vogels added, “has a democratisation effect”.

2. Every system will defend itself

His second prediction is about security, and he frames it as already happening. “In 2027, adversarial testing will move into every phase of software development,” said Vogels. “When WannaCry spread through systems around the world in 2017, it ran on an exploit stolen from the NSA and struck 59 days after a patch was available.”

That head start has gone, he said. “Agents now bring expertise with them, run in swarms, and are becoming so cheap that the cost of running hundreds of them in parallel is negligible for an attacker,” explained Vogels.

In April, Anthropic pointed “1,000 copies of Claude” at OpenBSD. Across 1,000 runs, the work cost less than $20,000, he said, and found a 27-year-old flaw in its TCP stack that could crash any host. The individual run that found it cost less than $50.

The answer, he said, is to run the same techniques in reverse before software ships. “Just like with Toyota’s Andon cord, which allows any employee to stop the line when a defect is found, they will prevent any known defect from shipping,” said Vogels.

Amazon already runs Autonomous Threat Analysis, where one group of tens of thousands of agents invents attacks and another tests whether defences catch them. “It’s still the humans that make decisions,” he said. “We will trust systems because the people who built them attacked them first.”

3. Sovereignty to become a non-functional requirement

Vogels’ third prediction is that sovereignty will move from an after-the-fact audit to a requirement designed in from the start, the way cost is handled in his Frugal Architect framework. Of its “seven laws”, the first says, “Cost becomes a non-functional requirement”. Sovereignty, he argues, should follow the same logic.

That means deciding encryption, key management and location up front, but also being able to change things. “Systems now change faster than any audit can follow,” he said. “An AI agent can add a replica in another region or swap a model in minutes.”

It comes down to risk analysis, said Vogels. “Organisations that wall off every workload in the most restrictive environment they can find and apply the same rules to a lunch menu as to a patient record will pay in cost, in resilience, and in access to new capabilities,” he said.

Frugality, added Vogels, was always about spending deliberately, because “isolation is not the same thing as control”.

Asked how sovereignty should be built in, he said teams must decide up front what restrictions apply to each class of data, and that the answer runs wider than where datacentres sit. “It’s not just about the location where the datacentres are,” said Vogels. “It is also about what services are available, what services do you rely on? Who do you trust?”

4. Scientists and agents will find new cures

Vogels’ fourth prediction is that researchers working with AI agents will find new treatments. Before becoming a technologist, he worked in cancer research. Vogels argued that treating disease as a single entity misses how differently it affects each person. “When we think about disease, we think about disease as an entity, but it’s not,” he said.

“Before this decade is out, scientists working with agents will discover a cure for a disease that today’s medicine can only manage,” added Vogels.

In August, in a late-stage melanoma trial, a personalised messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) cancer vaccine used with pembrolizumab cut the risk of recurrence and distant metastasis compared with using pembrolizumab alone, with machine learning selecting the vaccine’s targets from each patient’s tumour.

Agents handle the brute-force search, said Vogels. “It’s not just looking for a needle in a haystack, it is 1,000 haystacks and there’s still only one needle,” he said. “It’s like having a door that’s locked, and you have a billion keys and you need to figure out which key will open this particular door. That’s just brute force work, and agents can help scientists with that brute force work.”

5. The mind will become readable

Vogels saved his favourite prediction for last. Namely, “the mind becomes readable”.

He called the brain “the most amazing machine in existence”, which we have forced to talk to the world through a keyboard, a mouse and touch. Implants already restore hearing and sight, but few healthy people want surgery.

“A 2024 YouGov survey found only one in five would consider a brain implant, and in the United States, that fell to 11%,” he said.

But the non-invasive route is advancing, added Vogels. This summer, researchers at Meta and several European labs used a magnetoencephalography scanner outside the skull to record the magnetic signals the brain produced as people typed.

“It reached 61% word accuracy on 90 hours of recordings, and kept improving as more data came in,” he said, citing a 50% improvement in some stroke therapies.

The money is following, added Vogels. In six months, Chinese companies in the field raised more than 4.6 billion yuan, while the UK is putting £69m into new neural interfaces.

What excites him, he said, is not command and control, but amplification. “Interfaces that let you catch an innovative idea at the edge of your mind before it’s gone,” said Vogels. “Instead of having to rely on a chatbot, maybe we should just supersize our brains with this technology. The most successful technologies we can build will be those that amplify our unique human skills.”

title: Third-party support: Risks and opportunities
raw_text:
Analyst Forrester has reported that with the ongoing global economic uncertainty, some organisations are avoiding allocating funds for large applications and business transformation efforts.

In its Third-party software support offers a low-cost alternative report, Forrester says those organisations with budgetary concerns are tightening IT spending for on-premise applications, and reserving funds for mandatory application upgrades and modernisations only. 

Due to inflation, Forrester notes that many software providers are increasing their annual maintenance and support fees for existing customers.

“Sometimes these increases occur every year, leading to a significant cumulative increase over time,” Forrester notes in the report.

There is also the use of the so-called “carrot or stick” technique, which Forrester says is often used by software providers to motivate their on-premise customers to move to a software as a service (SaaS) or hosted cloud offering.

Forrester’s research shows that in the enterprise software market, the global move to the cloud is steady, but it’s not as rapid as for non-enterprise software.

This, according to Forrester, puts an additional burden on software providers to maintain technical, functional, product and security personnel to support older software versions. “For customers that don’t have price protection language in their contracts or see no way to avoid the certainty of cost increases, moving to TPSS [third-party support service] is a viable alternative with comprehensive SLAs [service-level agreements],” the analyst states.

Read more about third party software support

  • Does third-party support make sense: We speak to a Rimini Street customer about their experience of managing an Oracle ERP.
  • How Specsavers saved on Oracle costs: The high street opticians chain has swapped Oracle support for Spinnaker third-party support to help drive its business transformation.

Cost savings can be significant, especially as IT departments can keep a stable enterprise system running using third-party support, while they focus on areas of the business to generate additional value, such as a new artificial intelligence (AI) initiative.

Cyber risks

But CIOs will need to be prepared to answer questions on how safe an enterprise system protected by third-party support can be, especially with the advent of AI-powered cyber attacks. If a cyber security patch is released or an advisory published on the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures database, hackers are alerted there is a known weakness in an enterprise system.

AI has made it possible to craft an exploit extremely quickly, often before IT admins have fully patched the vulnerable systems. IT departments can only download patches from their enterprise software provider so long as they have an active support contract.

If support is provided by a third party, access to that patch is simply not available or not authorised. An IT department downloading patches it is officially no longer able to licence risks incurring a software piracy claim.

According to James Harvey, chief technology officer at Rimini Street for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, IT departments are thinking differently about their technology stack than they did decades ago, especially with the introduction of modern, cloud-native architectures, which influences how they consider the support of enterprise software.

“I think the concept of patching, as we’ve known it for the best part of 30 to 40 years, is changing,” he said. “As we see enterprises construct IT differently, using less fully packaged applications, and more containerised microservices with multiple landing zones, there is less of a system of record that may lose their data. Instead, they have a very wide federated data model across multiple applications.”

Since their customers no longer have access to the patches supplied by enterprise software providers, third-party support providers need to take a different approach to securing their customers’ IT systems. “We have an organisation internally that enables our customers to harden everything around their enterprise system,” said Harvey. “Rather than a patch that works from the technology up, we harden IT security from the business down.”

“You’re still getting the same protection, but in a different way,” he said. “It’s not less secure. It’s as good – if not better – and it’s as safe.”

Due to inflation, Forrester notes that many software providers are increasing their annual maintenance and support fees for existing customers.

“Sometimes these increases occur every year, leading to a significant cumulative increase over time,” Forrester notes in the report.

There is also the use of the so-called “carrot or stick” technique, which Forrester says is often used by software providers to motivate their on-premise customers to move to a software as a service (SaaS) or hosted cloud offering.

Forrester’s research shows that in the enterprise software market, the global move to the cloud is steady, but it’s not as rapid as for non-enterprise software.

This, according to Forrester, puts an additional burden on software providers to maintain technical, functional, product and security personnel to support older software versions. “For customers that don’t have price protection language in their contracts or see no way to avoid the certainty of cost increases, moving to TPSS [third-party support service] is a viable alternative with comprehensive SLAs [service-level agreements],” the analyst states.

title: Peer calls on prime minister to intervene in DWP subpostmaster prosecutions review
raw_text:
UK prime minister Andy Burnham is being urged to intervene and deliver the promised government review of subpostmaster prosecutions by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Peer Prem Sikka has written to Burnham asking him to personally end the “unacceptable” delay to a review that was first promised nearly two years ago.

Around 100 subpostmasters and branch staff were prosecuted by the DWP with support from the Post Office. Following the increased public awareness of the Post Office scandal, which included hundreds of wrongful subpostmaster convictions, the government said it would review the DWP prosecutions in February 2025.

Speaking on behalf of the government in the House of Lords at the time, peer Maggie Jones, in response to a question from fellow peer Prem Sikka, said: “My noble friend Lord Sikka raised a question about the DWP convictions. I can assure him that the minister for transformation is looking into this, a review is being established, and I hope to provide more information about that.”

In his letter to Burnham, Sikka wrote: “I am writing to urge you to intervene to ensure the government’s promises are delivered.”

He added: “My focus is on the 100 or so prosecutions of subpostmasters by the DWP, dating back to 1996. Despite an announcement of a review 21 months ago, nothing has happened.”

In August 2026, the government had not yet appointed a reviewer of the cases. According to a freedom of information response at the time, 113 people applied for the position, which will look at the prosecutions of subpostmasters by the DWP between 1996 and 2018.

A DWP spokesperson said: “We remain committed to an independent review of the department’s approach, and will update on the appointment of a reviewer in due course.”

The DWP said these were complex investigations backed by evidence including surveillance, stolen benefit books and handwriting analysis, and that decisions on convictions were for the courts, not DWP. It added that the review will assess the steps DWP took to gather and review information on Horizon-period prosecutions, and whether more could have been done to strengthen that work.

Focus turned on the DWP after the Post Office Horizon controversy hit the mainstream following an ITV drama about the scandal, which saw hundreds of subpostmasters wrongly prosecuted following account shortfalls.

These discrepancies were caused by errors in the Post Office Horizon system used in branches and affected thousands of subpostmasters. More than 900 subpostmaster convictions, which had been based on data from Horizon, were overturned en masse through an act of Parliament in May 2024.

The DWP worked with the Post Office on its subpostmaster prosecutions, and it has emerged that prosecutions of people using various systems at Post Office branches could also be flawed.

In January 2026, Neil Hudgell, lawyer at Hudgell Solicitors, told Computer Weekly that his law firm is pursuing its own investigations on behalf of clients and already had “a couple of cases lined up” to send to the CCRC.

“We’ve unearthed some interesting things that we think impact the safety of convictions, so we’re not waiting around on DWP themselves,” said Hudgell. “Someone needs to lean on the DWP, because it’s not good enough. [The longer it takes], the more suspicion subpostmasters have that there’s something to hide.”

summary:
UK prime minister Andy Burnham is being urged to intervene and deliver the promised government review of subpostmaster prosecutions by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Peer Prem Sikka has written to Burnham asking him to personally end the “unacceptable” delay to a review that was first promised nearly two years ago.

Around 100 subpostmasters and branch staff were prosecuted by the DWP with support from the Post Office. Following the increased public awareness of the Post Office scandal, which included hundreds of wrongful subpostmaster convictions, the government said it would review the DWP prosecutions in February 2025.

Speaking on behalf of the government in the House of Lords at the time, peer Maggie Jones, in response to a question from fellow peer Prem Sikka, said: “My noble friend Lord Sikka raised a question about the DWP convictions. I can assure him that the minister for transformation is looking into this, a review is being established, and I hope to provide more information about that.”

In his letter to Burnham, Sikka wrote: “I am writing to urge you to intervene to ensure the government’s promises are delivered.”

He added: “My focus is on the 100 or so prosecutions of subpostmasters by the DWP, dating back to 1996. Despite an announcement of a review 21 months ago, nothing has happened.”

In August 2026, the government had not yet appointed a reviewer of the cases. According to a freedom of information response at the time, 113 people applied for the position, which will look at the prosecutions of subpostmasters by the DWP between 1996 and 2018.

A DWP spokesperson said: “We remain committed to an independent review of the department’s approach, and will update on the appointment of a reviewer in due course.”

The DWP said these were complex investigations backed by evidence including surveillance, stolen benefit books and handwriting analysis, and that decisions on convictions were for the courts, not DWP.

title: UK cyber legislation fails to tackle real-world resilience
raw_text:
From mid-July through into October, more than a fair amount of my House of Lords colleagues' and my time has been filled with trying to improve the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill (CSRB). A milestone, of sorts, came when the bill passed its third reading on 2 November.

The bill will be considered in the House of Commons today (24 November) with over 100 amendments, 64 of which dropped from the government a day before we were due to begin our detailed consideration - sweet timing? Even with so many changes, the bill is significantly insufficient in so many critical areas.

Shaking up cyber law

For security leaders across the UK, the legislation represents the biggest shake-up to the Network and Information Systems (NIS) regulations since 2018.

Originally introduced in November 2025 and carried over between parliamentary sessions, the bill aims to close gaps that have widened as attackers target interconnected supply chains. It pulls managed service providers (MSPs), datacentres, large load-controllers, and designated critical suppliers into regulatory scope alongside essential operators in energy, water, transport, health, and digital infrastructure.

It also compresses incident reporting to an initial alert within 24 hours and a fuller report within 72, grants ministers powers to issue directions, allows regulators to recover costs, and raises maximum penalties up to £17m or 4% of global turnover.

All of this is very much known. What remains at best opaque is what the Commons will make of the amended bill and what happens when it begins its staggered roll-out, still with so many gaps.

Real-world resilience

There will be much ado about regulation through 2027 and 2028, but will this be enough and in time? To answer with brevity, at this stage, I offer just a few short words to contemplate - and they would be: impact on real-world resilience.

From my perspective, we were able to get two important changes through at report stage on 26 October. First, forcing a 12-month review of the NIS regime, and second, a register of state actors posing cyber threats to the UK. We must wait to see what ministers will make of this.

Even when royal assent finally arrives, professional practitioners in the security field point to a long list of gaps that the bill leaves unresolved. We tried.

Perhaps the most glaring omission is who finds themselves outside the imposed perimeter.

While expanding into MSPs and datacentres addresses a major weakness in the digital supply chain, the framework remains restricted to essential services and designated critical suppliers.

Outside the perimeter

As our House of Lords National Resilience Select Committee has recently rightly warned, major commercial enterprises find themselves outside that perimeter. Retail is currently out. Think about the terrible time we all shared during Covid. Retail is significant, some might even suggest critical - I would.

Similarly, last year’s Jaguar Land Rover cyber attack had a catastrophic impact that went throughout the motor industry supply chain, bleeding out into the wider economy and registering in a reduction to that quarter’s GDP. Is a cyber attack in the motor industry, impacting GDP, significant? Critical?

The 24-hour and 72-hour reporting requirements were, well, very much reported upon. But is there any necessarily helpful link between the rapidity of the reporting and that of the recovery? Colleagues and I at both committee and report stages of the legislation continued to make these points to little or no avail.

Read more about the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill

  • MPs propose ‘kill switch’ to shut down rogue AI systems - An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill proposes giving the government a ‘kill switch’ to close datacentres hosting AI if they pose a critical threat to UK infrastructure or national security.
  • Are we mistaking regulation for resilience? We have a growing number of cyber compliance regulations, yet our country’s cyber resilience remains fragile. What is going wrong?
  • IT services companies and datacentres face regulation as cyber security bill reaches Parliament - The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will require large IT services companies, including datacentres, to report security incidents within 24 hours.

Though the bill is clear on the clocks, it is less so when it comes to who is responsible for fixing underlying vulnerabilities or how remediation must be carried out.

We debated at length issues around board accountability, senior competence and more - all left out. There is nothing currently on the face of the bill in primary legislation - all is left, at best, to regulation.

And what of skills, training, development and recruitment in the first instance? Industry research has regularly highlighted widespread cyber skills shortages across UK organisations and public bodies, set alongside a surge in reported cyber incidents.

And spare a thought for the smaller firms in the supply chain facing a double squeeze - even if not regulated directly, they will feel pressure through stricter contracts and procurement rules.

We tried over several sessions to secure a dedicated national cyber support service for small and medium-sized businesses. Sensible – but not accepted.

Regulating emerging technologies

The bill also leaves structural questions hanging over enforcement and emerging tech.

Our efforts to stand up a single cyber security regulator to end cross-sector inconsistency were dashed by the government’s preference for a sectoral model, leaving organisations navigating different regulators in varying degrees of fog.

This allies clearly with calls I have made for years now on the need for a single, right-sized, horizontally focused AI regulator - so it should be with cyber and yet, in the UK as a consequence of this bill, it is not.

The entire kennel of dogs that fail to bark in this bill are all things AI. Despite some of the government’s late amendments sort of nodding, hinting, muttering towards this or, at times proxying, it is still extraordinary that, as AI features in so many cyber attacks, the bill seems so very oblivious to this. We tried.

We were also informed that a cyber bill was not the right place to put in the painfully overdue protections for our good-faith cyber professionals who do so much to keep us safe, often and understandably out of sight.

As the bill reappears in the Commons today, the immediate question is what the government will do with the amendments we got through in October. It’s safe to say that we will be seeing the bill again shortly and will continue to push on many of these issues.

Issues unaddressed

The CSRB will, eventually, receive royal assent, that is not in doubt. What is far less clear is how the raft of regulations will be brought in and at what pace.

With so many critical issues left unaddressed, there is one thing we can be clear on - the resulting Cyber Security and Resilience Act will have avoidably missed significant matters which would have made it far more coherent, created greater coverage and kept more sectors and more of us safe from the cyber onslaught.

Perhaps this bill, shortly to become an act, is not so much an iron dome - more an upturned colander?

title: Huang’s Trump-backed return raises AI sovereignty concerns
raw_text:
Just a week ago, during its third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia’s chairman described co-founder Jensen Huang’s behaviour as “inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms”.

Yet Huang is now back as CEO, thanks to US president Donald Trump’s direct intervention. His return leaves many questions unanswered, particularly relating to the influence of the White House on a private company and export controls and how these could be used by the US government to curb the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) acceleration technology in countries where it wants to exert influence.

During the earning call on 17 November, chairman of the board, Harvey Jones, said: “On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Huang’s departure saw the share price of the AI chipmaker plummet. His reinstatement led to shares in the company rallying.

Jones refused to take any questions regarding the former CEO during the call, but said the board acted deliberately and in the best interests of employees, customers, partners and shareholders. Yet just a week later, following what appears to be pressure from the White House, he said: “The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia , and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

In a statement, Nvidia said that the board had received input from senior levels of the United States government and, based on that input, it was confident that Huang’s reinstatement would not pose a national security risk.

Huang’s reinstatement illustrates the strong links between the US administration and the chipmaker, and raises concerns over access to advanced AI chips should the White House choose to exert influence.

Forrester’s vice-president and group research director, Stephanie Balaouras, said the reinstatement of Huang as CEO may calm immediate concerns, but the concentration risk for businesses still remains: “The news changes the leadership picture, but not the strategic advice. The concentration risk still remains what it is.

“While Huang’s reinstatement may calm immediate concerns around Nvidia’s leadership, it should not reverse enterprise efforts to build alternatives into their AI infrastructure strategy. Restoring leadership does not mean restoring confidence in resilience. Leaders need to keep confronting AI concentration risk.”

It has been widely reported that Huang had an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore datacentre firm Megaspeed, which has been an Nvidia partner since 2023, leading to his decision to step down.

The Singapore link

Writing on LinkedIn, former US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) attorney John Reed Stark questioned the accuracy of Nvidia’s quarterly earnings filings. In the post, he pointed to the company’s fiscal 2023 filing through the first half of fiscal 2026. Stark said Nvidia’s annual report (10-K) and quarterly filings (10-Q) attributed roughly $52bn of revenue to Singapore, a city-state of about six million people.

“That total is my own addition to the figures in those filings,” he said. “Nvidia never published it as a single number. Nvidia explained in its footnotes that Singapore was mostly an invoicing address and that the chips went somewhere else. Then, one quarter after Nvidia reportedly put its largest Southeast Asian customer on an internal block list, the Singapore line disappeared from the filings altogether. The revenue did not. Nvidia had switched to reporting by customer headquarters, and the totals stayed the same.”

The US Department of Commerce began an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list.

Powerful AI chip restrictions

On 16 November, the US Department of Commerce department the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published interim final rule entitled Addressing remote access to advanced semiconductors, which will require a licence to export, re-export or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil.

The interim final rule from BIS states: “You may not knowingly export, re-export or transfer (in-county) [advanced computer chips] for use in a datacentre to or within any destination worldwide that will provide access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP (total processing performance).” This TPP figure roughly equates to approximately 760 Nvidia H100 graphics processor units (GPUs).

While the restrictions do not apply to the UK, the Isambard-AI supercomputer in Bristol contains 5,448 Nvidia H100 GPUs integrated inside 5,448 Nvidia GH200 Grace Hopper, representing approximately 86 million TPP.

Commenting on the return of Huang, Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello said: “The company will face restrictions in selling leading artificial intelligence gear to countries (mostly in Southeast Asia) that were renting cloud workloads to Chinese AI model builders.

“The US government will undoubtedly have closer eyes on Nvidia, including a Securities and Exchange Commission accounting investigation. The US has made it clear that it considers Nvidia’s gear as a sort of weapon subject to regulation, and the firm will have to navigate this accordingly.”

Along with Alice Huang’s connection to Megaspeed, the US Department of Justice has been looking at whether she tried using US-based Super Micro to export servers equipped with AI acceleration chips indirectly to China.

Just a week ago, during its third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia’s chairman described co-founder Jensen Huang’s behaviour as “inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms”.

Yet Huang is now back as CEO, thanks to US president Donald Trump’s direct intervention. His return leaves many questions unanswered, particularly relating to the influence of the White House on a private company and export controls and how these could be used by the US government to curb the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) acceleration technology in countries where it wants to exert influence.

During the earning call on 17 November, chairman of the board, Harvey Jones, said: “On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Huang’s departure saw the share price of the AI chipmaker plummet. His reinstatement led to shares in the company rallying.

Jones refused to take any questions regarding the former CEO during the call, but said the board acted deliberately and in the best interests of employees, customers, partners and shareholders.

title: Post Office to meet former subpostmaster over redress scheme disagreement
raw_text:
The Post Office has agreed to meet a former subpostmaster and his legal representative over concerns that redress schemes have not included potentially large volumes of branch losses.

Denis O’Donnell, who, for decades, ran a branch in Prestatyn, Wales, will meet the Post Office over his assertion that, despite promises, it has not properly alerted subpostmasters to an operational issue he first highlighted in 2019 that caused unexplained losses.

As a result, the former subpostmaster said that the closure of redress schemes means subpostmasters won’t be repaid the money they spent covering losses that were not their fault.

O’Donnell had originally informed the Post Office about a problem in 2019, but said he was “fobbed off”. But after pressure from Computer Weekly and forensic investigator Ron Warmington last year, the Post Office eventually investigated the issue and acknowledged it could cause unexplained losses.

Read more about O’Donnell’s revelation: Post Office scandal investigator warns public inquiry about Horizon defect at large for years

The issue, branded the “part payments” defect, was likely to have seen some customers, for decades, receive extra cash from subpostmasters without realising.

A Horizon screen icon that allowed subpostmasters to both take money and pay money was at the centre of the issue. When multiple transactions, including in and out payments, are held at the same time in what is known as a “stack”, Horizon could make a payment to the customer but record it as a payment to the branch, therefore creating an instant discrepancy.

In a push to get the Post Office to investigate further, O’Donnell will meet some of its executives, alongside Flora Page, a barrister who has played a central role in overturning wrongful subpostmaster convictions.

The Post Office confirmed the meeting but had nothing to add. It has previously said: “It is impossible to know the exact impact in the network [of the issue] and we acknowledge there will be subpostmasters who have experienced the issue and not raised it. But we do believe the overall impact is limited. The number of discrepancies in a year attributed to this process is 10 out of 14,000, or 0.07%, where discrepancies have been made known to us via our Review and Dispute button on Horizon.”

O’Donnell believes the Post Office is underestimating the issue. He said he raised the issue with the Post Office seven-and-a-half years ago, but it did nothing. He added that the problem had likely existed over a decade before he alerted the organisation. “I want the Post Office to fully admit to this problem,” said O’Donnell.

Page said: “It is encouraging that the Post Office has agreed to meet with Mr O’Donnell and me. We will have to wait and see whether they take appropriate action thereafter.”

Read more about O’Donnell’s campaign

It was after a 2018 High Court trial that the Post Office acknowledged it had wrongly blamed subpostmasters for account shortfalls caused by errors in the Horizon computer system and established its first redress scheme, known as the Horizon Shortfalls Scheme. Others have followed, including a scheme for those wrongfully convicted of crimes.

A scheme was later set up for subpostmasters who had experienced unexplained losses as a result of shortfalls caused by Post Office processes rather than computer-related errors, known as the Post Office Process Review (PPR).

This scheme was closed at the end of September 2026, despite calls from O’Donnell for an extension because he believed subpostmasters had not been properly alerted to an operational defect he identified.

Read more: Post Office Horizon scandal explained: Everything you need to know

In October 2025, after the issue was revealed, the Post Office told Computer Weekly: “We would like to assure your readers that Post Office today has taken this matter seriously… We encourage any current or former postmaster who believes they may have been impacted by this issue to get in touch as they may be eligible for redress through the PPR.”

The Post Office has since stated that people who experienced the “part payments” defect, without understanding it, may have been compensated through the £75,000 fixed sum in the Horizon Shortfall Scheme (HSS).

O’Donnell does not believe the Post Office has done enough to encourage subpostmasters to come forward in relation to what forensic investigator Warmington described as an “operational defect”. He fears that many subpostmasters have missed out on what they are owed.

The former subpostmaster himself made a claim in the PPR scheme, which included “part payments” defect losses, but the Post Office made no offer based on claims related to the “part payments” defect.

Wider redress gap

Separately, there are more former subpostmasters and family members who could miss out on financial redress owed to them by the Post Office due to the passage of time.

Many had problems decades ago – some have suffered illness, and others have died in the years since, but new cases are emerging, and some deserving of redress could miss out unless the rules are changed.

Former subpostmasters were entitled to a £75,000 fixed sum award under the HSS if they had evidence of any unexplained shortfalls. This particular redress scheme has paid out over £1bn to subpostmasters.

The statutory public inquiry into the scandal agreed to a deadline of midnight on 27 November 2025, after which no claims for financial redress under HSS could be made. The Post Office accepted this recommendation, but decided on a later date of 31 January 2026. However, Computer Weekly has spoken to elderly former subpostmasters who were not even aware of the redress scheme until it was too late to apply and had their applications rejected. Others have only discovered letters from the Post Office after the death of their former subpostmaster parents.

Read more: Lost in the post: Subpostmasters could miss out on redress

Robert Nichol, a former subpostmaster who ran a Post Office branch in the village of Dalston, Cumbria, from 1982 to 2004, said he and his wife, Anne Nichol, had problems with Horizon, with regular unexplainable shortfalls after being forced to replace paper-based accounting methods with the software in 2000. By 2004, he resigned as a subpostmaster because “he just couldn’t cope with Horizon anymore”, said his wife.

Now, they face being excluded from financial redress schemes. Anne Nichol said the couple, who have moved several times since giving up their branch, never received any correspondence from the Post Office about applying for redress, and when they eventually applied to the Horizon Shortfalls Scheme in March, they were rejected. The Post Office claims it sent letters to Mr Nichol.

The first letter sent by the Nichols claiming redress was on 30 March, just two months after HSS closed for new applications. “We’ve got eight emails of rejection, all saying the same thing,” Mrs Nichol told Computer Weekly.

The Post Office has agreed to meet a former subpostmaster and his legal representative over concerns that redress schemes have not included potentially large volumes of branch losses.

Denis O’Donnell, who, for decades, ran a branch in Prestatyn, Wales, will meet the Post Office over his assertion that, despite promises, it has not properly alerted subpostmasters to an operational issue he first highlighted in 2019 that caused unexplained losses.

As a result, the former subpostmaster said that the closure of redress schemes means subpostmasters won’t be repaid the money they spent covering losses that were not their fault.

O’Donnell had originally informed the Post Office about a problem in 2019, but said he was “fobbed off”. But after pressure from Computer Weekly and forensic investigator Ron Warmington last year, the Post Office eventually investigated the issue and acknowledged it could cause unexplained losses.

Read more about O’Donnell’s revelation: Post Office scandal investigator warns public inquiry about Horizon defect at large for years

The issue, branded the “part payments” defect, was likely to have seen some customers, for decades, receive extra cash from subpostmasters without realising.

A Horizon screen icon that allowed subpostmasters to both take money and pay money was at the centre of the issue. When multiple transactions, including in and out payments, are held at the same time in what is known as a “stack”, Horizon could make a payment to the customer but record it as a payment to the branch, therefore creating an instant discrepancy.

In a push to get the Post Office to investigate further, O’Donnell will meet some of its executives, alongside Flora Page, a barrister who has played a central role in overturning wrongful subpostmaster convictions.

The Post Office confirmed the meeting but had nothing to add. It has previously said: “It is impossible to know the exact impact in the network [of the issue] and we acknowledge there will be subpostmasters who have experienced the issue and not raised it.

title: Software engineering is dead - long live software engineering
raw_text:
For most of my career, when anyone asked what I did, my answer was simple: "I'm a software engineer”. It covered research, product development, and the years I spent in senior roles helping large organisations fix the way they delivered software at scale.

At some point I stopped saying it.

That was not because I think the role matters less. Quite the opposite. I stopped because the characteristics and skills the label describes had changed beyond all recognition, and the words no longer told people what the work actually involves.

This matters now because, once again, we are being told that software engineering is finished. The latest culprit is "vibe coding". Before accepting the obituary, it is worth remembering how many times it has been written before.

‘Reports of my death are greatly exaggerated’

Mark Twain once had to point out that reports of his death had been premature. Software engineering has had to do the same, repeatedly.

The promise of a shortcut to high-quality software is as old as the industry itself. In 1981 a small Somerset company, D.J. "AI" Systems, released a program generator it called The last one, on the basis that it would be the last program a human would ever need to write.

A year later James Martin, one of the most influential IT thinkers of the era, published Application development without programmers, arguing that fourth-generation languages and application generators would put development into the hands of users.

The pattern repeated through the decades that followed. Computer-aided software engineering (CASE) tools in the late 1980s promised to generate systems directly from structured analysis diagrams. Model-driven architecture in the 2000s promised that precise specifications would be transformed automatically into working code. More recently, low-code and no-code platforms promised an army of citizen developers who would make the professional largely redundant.

Each wave delivered something real. Each also ran into the same wall. As Fred Brooks argued in his 1986 essay No silver bullet, tools attack the accidental complexity of software - the effort of expressing a design in a machine-readable form. They do very little about the essential complexity - deciding what the system should do, how it should behave when things go wrong, and how it will evolve. That essential work is what software engineering has always been about.

Much of my time at IBM, and my book Enterprise software delivery, went on arguing that the real gains come from engineering the delivery system around the code, not from any single tool.

Vibe coding: The latest pronouncement

In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy, a founding member of OpenAI and former head of AI at Tesla, described a new way of programming in which you "fully give in to the vibes" and forget that the code even exists. You describe what you want, accept what the AI produces, and paste any error messages back in until it works.

The term spread fast because it named something many people were already doing. It also revived a familiar claim - if anyone can describe an app in plain English and have it built in minutes, why do we need software engineers at all?

“Someone still has to decide what the system should do, understand the context it operates in, judge the trade-offs, and take responsibility when it fails”

Alan Brown

The adoption figures make the claim feel plausible. Industry surveys quoted in a recent Google whitepaper suggest that around 85% of professional developers now use AI coding agents regularly and that roughly 41% of new code is AI-generated, although those numbers come from vendor sources and should be treated with some caution.

And yet, just as with The last one and its successors, the more closely you look at how serious organisations build software with these tools, the less the obituary holds up.

What the builders are actually describing

That Google whitepaper, The new SDLC (software development lifecycle) with vibe coding, is a useful lens precisely because it comes from people selling the new tools. Read it carefully and it is not a eulogy for software engineering - it is a description of software engineering being rebuilt around a new kind of component.

Three ideas stand out. First, the authors treat vibe coding and what they call "agentic engineering" as two ends of a spectrum, and the thing that places you on it is not the AI you use but how its output is verified. Without automated tests for the deterministic parts and human-driven structured evaluations for the rest, they argue, the practice remains vibe coding however clever the prompts.

Second, they offer a simple equation: agent = model + harness. The model is the engine. The harness is everything around it - rule files that encode conventions and constraints, tool definitions, sandboxed execution environments, orchestration logic, deterministic hooks that block a bad commit, and observability that shows what the agent did and why. They report that changing only the harness, with no change of model, moved one coding agent from outside the top 30 to the top five on a public benchmark.

Third, they describe a "factory model" in which the developer's primary output is no longer code but the system that produces code - specifications, agents, tests and quality gates, feedback loops and guardrails. Readers with long memories will recognise them. These are configuration management, requirements engineering, test automation, continuous integration and quality assurance, given new names and pointed at a new kind of worker.

The whitepaper is also candid about the limits. It cites a METR study in which experienced developers using AI assistants took around 19% longer on certain tasks, largely because of the effort spent verifying and correcting the output. It describes an "80% problem", where agents produce most of a feature quickly but the edge cases, error handling and integration points still demand deep contextual knowledge. And it warns that vibe coding looks cheap at the start but carries a compounding cost in token spend, maintenance and security remediation.

The closing line puts it well - generation is solved; verification, judgment and direction are the new craft.

What’s changed, and what’s not

None of this means nothing has changed. Three shifts are real, and they explain why I no longer use the old job title.

The first is the unit of work. Software engineers once spent most of their effort writing and debugging code. Increasingly, they design and tune the environment in which agents write code, and they move between directing an agent line by line and delegating whole tasks to agents working in the background.

The second is where the hard thinking sits. When implementation can be compressed from weeks to hours, the bottleneck moves to specification and verification. A well-written test and evaluation suite becomes the contract with the machine, a more precise statement of intent than any prompt. This is not a new insight, but it is now an unavoidable one.

The third is the economics. The trade-off between upfront investment in structure and the ongoing cost of running, fixing and maintaining software has always existed. AI makes it visible on a monthly token bill, and it rewards the organisations that invest early in context, tests and guardrails.

What has not changed is Brooks's essential complexity. Someone still has to decide what the system should do, understand the context it operates in, judge the trade-offs, and take responsibility when it fails.

Agentic AI doesn’t remove that work. It amplifies the consequences of doing it well or badly, because an agent will faithfully implement a poor specification at remarkable speed. That is why software engineering, understood as a discipline rather than a job title, is more important now than it has ever been.

Long live software engineering

Every previous announcement of the death of software engineering ended the same way. The tools were absorbed, the hype faded, and the discipline adapted to make use of what was genuinely new. I expect the same this time, with one difference - the speed of the change leaves far less room for organisations that treat AI coding as a productivity feature rather than an engineering investment.

The job title may have faded. The discipline has never mattered more.

He has spent more than 30 years in the US, Europe and the UK driving large-scale software-driven programmes with commercial high-tech companies, leading R&D teams, building state-of-the-art solutions and improving software product delivery approaches.
